section.title: The Anointing and the Triumphal Entry
section.sectionRationale: This chapter turns the Gospel toward the cross. Mary pours out costly perfume on Jesus, unknowingly preparing Him for burial, while Judas objects. The crowds hail Him as King entering Jerusalem on a donkey, and the arrival of Greeks seeking Jesus signals that His hour has finally come. Jesus speaks of the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit, of being lifted up to draw all people, and closes His public ministry with a summons to believe in the light before the darkness falls.
section.thesis: As Mary's extravagant devotion anoints Him for burial and the crowds hail Him as King, Jesus announces that His hour has come to be glorified, the hour of a grain of wheat falling to die and bear much fruit, of being lifted up to draw all people and cast out the prince of this world, so that His public ministry ends with a final call to believe in the light.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Mary's anointing and Judas's objection; the plot against Lazarus; the triumphal entry of the King on a donkey; the coming of the Greeks and the hour of the grain of wheat and the lifting up; and the verdict of unbelief and Jesus' closing appeal to believe in the light.

units.label: Mary anoints Jesus
units.note: kept for the day of My burial

verses.text: Six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, the hometown of Lazarus, whom He had raised from the dead.
So they hosted a dinner for Jesus there. Martha served, and Lazarus was among those reclining at the table with Him.
Then Mary took about a pint of expensive perfume, made of pure nard, and she anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped them with her hair. And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.
But one of His disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was going to betray Him, asked,
“Why wasn’t this perfume sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?”
Judas did not say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief. As keeper of the money bag, he used to take from what was put into it.
“Leave her alone,” Jesus replied. “She has kept this perfume in preparation for the day of My burial.
The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me.”

units.label: The plot to kill Lazarus
units.note: a living sign the leaders cannot bear

verses.text: Meanwhile a large crowd of Jews learned that Jesus was there. And they came not only because of Him, but also to see Lazarus, whom He had raised from the dead.
So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well,
for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus.

units.label: The triumphal entry
units.note: Blessed is the King of Israel

verses.text: The next day the great crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.
They took palm branches and went out to meet Him, shouting: “Hosanna!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the King of Israel!”
Finding a young donkey, Jesus sat on it, as it is written:
“Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.”

At first His disciples did not understand these things, but after Jesus was glorified they remembered what had been done to Him, and they realized that these very things had also been written about Him.
Meanwhile, many people who had been with Jesus when He called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to testify.
That is also why the crowd went out to meet Him, because they heard that He had performed this sign.
Then the Pharisees said to one another, “You can see that this is doing you no good. Look how the whole world has gone after Him!”

units.label: The hour of the grain of wheat
units.note: lifted up to draw all people

verses.text: Now there were some Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast.
They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and requested of him, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.”
Philip relayed this appeal to Andrew, and both of them went and told Jesus.
But Jesus replied, “The {{hora|hour}} has come for the Son of Man to be {{doxazo|glorified}}.
Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.
If anyone serves Me, he must follow Me; and where I am, My servant will be as well. If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him.
Now My soul is troubled, and what shall I say? ‘Father, save Me from this hour’? No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour.
Father, glorify Your name!” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
The crowd standing there heard it and said that it had thundered. Others said that an angel had spoken to Him.
In response, Jesus said, “This voice was not for My benefit, but yours.
Now judgment is upon this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out.
And I, when I am {{hupsoo|lifted up}} from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.”
He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die.
The crowd replied, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ will remain forever. So how can You say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”

Then Jesus told them, “For a little while longer, the Light will be among you. Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.
While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” After Jesus had spoken these things, He went away and was hidden from them.

units.label: Belief and unbelief
units.note: I have come as a light into the world

verses.text: Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him.
This was to fulfill the word of Isaiah the prophet: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”
For this reason they were unable to believe. For again, Isaiah says:
“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they cannot see with their eyes, and understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.”
Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him.
Nevertheless, many of the leaders believed in Him. But because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue.
For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.
Then Jesus cried out, “Whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me.
And whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me.
I have come into the world as a {{phos|light}}, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness.
As for anyone who hears My words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. For I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world.
There is a judge for the one who rejects Me and does not receive My words: The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.
I have not spoken on My own, but the Father who sent Me has commanded Me what to say and how to say it.
And I know that His command leads to eternal life. So I speak exactly what the Father has told Me to say.”

hora.gloss: Hour, the appointed time. Throughout John Jesus has said His hour had not yet come; now, with Greeks seeking Him, He announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. The long-awaited hour is the time of His death, resurrection, and exaltation, and from here the Gospel moves steadily toward it.

doxazo.gloss: To glorify, to reveal or bestow glory. Strikingly, the Son of Man is glorified not in escaping death but in dying; the cross is His glorification. The Father answers Jesus' prayer, glorify Your name, with the promise, I will glorify it again. In John the deepest glory of God shines precisely at the cross.

hupsoo.gloss: To lift up, exalt. As with Nicodemus and the serpent, the word carries a double sense: Jesus is lifted up on the cross and thereby lifted up in exaltation. John notes plainly that He said this to indicate the kind of death He would die. The lifting up is the means by which He draws all people to Himself.

phos.gloss: Light. Jesus, the light of the world, presses a final appeal: walk while you have the light, believe in the light, become sons of light. The light will be among them only a little longer, so the time to respond is now, before the darkness falls; to believe in the light is to be rescued from the dark.

basic.context: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany, Mary pours a fortune of perfume over Jesus' feet. Judas objects, feigning concern for the poor, but Jesus defends her: she has kept it for His burial. The next day the crowds welcome Jesus into Jerusalem as King, waving palms and quoting Scripture, though the disciples understand only later. When some Greeks come seeking Jesus, He announces that His hour has come, and speaks of a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit, and of being lifted up to draw all people. His public ministry closes with a plea to believe in the light before the darkness comes.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter is a threshold: the public ministry ends and the Passion begins. Mary's lavish act models wholehearted devotion, over against Judas's calculating greed. The triumphal entry shows Jesus deliberately coming as the humble King of Zechariah's prophecy. The arrival of Greeks triggers the announcement of the hour, hinting that His death will gather the nations. The grain of wheat and the lifting up interpret His death in advance. The key question is whether we, like the crowd, will believe in the light while we still have it.
basic.originalLanguages: Several key terms converge. Jesus announces that the hora, the hour, has come for the Son of Man to be doxazo, glorified, meaning glorified through death. He will be hupsoo, lifted up, on the cross, and so draw all people to Himself. And He makes a final appeal to believe in the phos, the light, before the darkness falls.
basic.typology: Mary's anointing prepares the King's body for burial, echoing the anointing of kings and pointing to the Messiah, the Anointed One. The entry on a donkey fulfills Zechariah's picture of the humble King. The grain of wheat that dies to bear fruit is a parable of the cross and the harvest of the nations.
basic.christ: Christ is the King who comes in humility, the grain of wheat who dies to bear much fruit, the one lifted up to draw all people and cast out the prince of this world, and the light who has come to save. His hour, long awaited, has arrived.
basic.god: God the Father glorifies His name through the Son, answering aloud from heaven. He is the God who saves the world through the Son's death, and whose word will finally judge those who reject it. Even human unbelief is woven into His sovereign plan foretold by Isaiah.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 9 foretells the King on a donkey. Psalm 118 supplies the Hosanna. Isaiah 53 and 6 are quoted on unbelief. John 3 first spoke of the lifting up of the Son of Man.
basic.oneStory: The King foretold by the prophets enters His city, not to seize a throne but to die like a grain of wheat and bear a harvest of all nations. Lifted up on the cross, He draws the world to Himself and casts out the prince of this world, and the coming of the Greeks signals that the ingathering of the nations has begun.

context.literary:
John 12 is built from pairs. Costly devotion sits beside calculating greed in verses 1 to 8. A crowd that wants to see Lazarus is set against priests who want him dead, verses 9 to 11. A procession of welcome is answered by a Pharisee's gloomy complaint, verses 12 to 19. The Greeks' request opens the hour, and unbelief and belief close the chapter, verses 37 to 50. John tells the story so that every scene shows two reactions to the same Jesus, and the reader is asked which one is theirs.

Lazarus is the thread through the opening half. He reclines at the table in verse 2, draws the crowd in verse 9, becomes a target in verse 10, and is the subject of the testimony in verse 17. The raising of chapter 11 is both what makes the welcome possible and what sharpens the plot, which is why John keeps naming him. Then the sign vocabulary returns in verses 18 and 37, and the second of these sums up the Book of Signs: so many signs, and still they did not believe.

Irony is the chapter's main device. The Pharisees say, 'Look how the whole world has gone after Him!' in verse 19, and in the very next verse the Greeks arrive. The crowd quotes a psalm about the one who comes in the Lord's name without knowing how the psalm will be fulfilled. Jesus then speaks of the world three times in quick succession, as the realm now under judgment, verse 31, and as the people He will draw to Himself, verse 32.

The second half works like John's Gethsemane. John gives no garden prayer later, but here Jesus says 'Now My soul is troubled' in verse 27 and refuses the easy prayer, 'Father, save Me from this hour.' After He withdraws and hides in verse 36, the narrator reflects on unbelief in verses 37 to 43, and then Jesus cries out again in verses 44 to 50. Most readers take that last speech as a summary of His whole public teaching rather than a fresh scene.
context.historical:
Bethany lay about two miles from Jerusalem, John 11:18, close enough for a Passover pilgrim to stay there. The city was swollen with visitors, which explains why a 'great crowd' was on hand to hear that Jesus was coming. The meal itself was a dinner at which guests reclined, and the family of Lazarus hosted it, which is why Martha serves, as she did in Luke 10:40.

The perfume was pure nard, an aromatic oil imported from far to the east, and the quantity was about a pint, in Greek a litra, roughly a Roman pound in weight. Judas prices it at three hundred denarii. A denarius was a labourer's daily wage, Matthew 20:2, so the jar was worth close to a year of ordinary work. Burial customs of the time included spices and ointments for the body, John 19:40, which gives Jesus' words about her act their sense.

Palm branches were the sign of joyous national celebration. They belonged to the pilgrim feasts, Leviticus 23:40, and were used when Israel hailed a victorious deliverer. 'Hosanna' began as a plea, 'Save, we pray,' Psalm 118:25, and by Jesus' day had become a shout of acclamation. The crowd's 'King of Israel' goes beyond the psalm; John has already used that title when Nathanael confessed Jesus, John 1:49.

The donkey carries a political meaning that is easy to miss. When David appointed Solomon his successor, Solomon rode into the city on the king's mule, 1 Kings 1:33. A king on a donkey was still a king, but one who came in peace and not in a war chariot. The Greeks who come to Philip were Gentiles who had travelled to worship at the feast. They could have stood in the outer court of the temple, which was the place assigned to Gentiles. Fear of being put out of the synagogue, verse 42, is a real social threat. John uses a single word for it, aposynagogos, in John 9:22, 12:42 and 16:2, and it carries the weight of losing one's whole community.
context.canonical:
John treats the chapter as the fulfillment of Scripture at nearly every turn. The entry quotes Zechariah 9:9 in condensed form, and its opening words, 'Do not be afraid,' echo the comfort of Zephaniah 3:16, 'Do not fear, O Zion,' so that the King's arrival carries both promise and reassurance. The shouts come from Psalm 118:25 and 26, the last of the Passover Hallel psalms, sung at the very feast that Jesus is about to fulfill.

The two Isaiah citations in verses 38 and 40 frame the chapter's verdict. The first, Isaiah 53:1, belongs to the Servant song that opens with the Servant 'raised and lifted up and highly exalted,' Isaiah 52:13, the very verbs behind John's lifted up. The second, Isaiah 6:10, comes from the call vision in which Isaiah saw the Lord's glory, and John says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory, verse 41. Paul quotes Isaiah 53:1 in Romans 10:16, and Isaiah 6:9 and 10 appear in Matthew 13:14 and 15, Mark 4:12, Luke 8:10 and Acts 28:26 and 27, so the early church read Israel's resistance as already foreseen.

The anointing at Bethany appears in Matthew 26:6 to 13 and Mark 14:3 to 9, where the woman pours the oil on His head, and Luke 7:36 to 50 records a different anointing of His feet in a Pharisee's house. John 11:2 had already introduced Mary as the one who anointed the Lord. The picture of a kernel that must die, verse 24, is taken up in Paul's teaching on the resurrection body, 1 Corinthians 15:36 to 38. The lifting up that draws all people ties back to John 3:14 and forward to Colossians 2:15, where the cross is a triumph over the powers.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants his readers to see that the cross is not an accident that overtakes Jesus but the purpose He walks toward. Each scene in the chapter interprets His death before it happens. Mary's oil reads it as a burial, the crowd's palms as a coronation, the grain of wheat as a fruitful dying, and the lifting up as a drawing of the nations. By the time the reader reaches the arrest, there are no surprises left in Jesus' mind, only fulfillment.

He also means to show that the response to Jesus divides people sharply, and that the dividing is not about knowledge. The crowds have seen the signs, the leaders believe in secret, and the Greeks ask to see Him. The question the chapter leaves with its readers is whether they will confess Him publicly, or, like the leaders in verse 43, love the praise of people more than the praise of God.

The Isaiah quotations are there to steady a church that was wondering why so many in Israel had not believed. John answers that this was foreseen, and that it does not make the message weaker. It is a pastoral comfort for those who preach to hard hearts, and a warning for those who hear.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes an anointing, a procession and a conversation. It does not make extravagance a rule. Jesus defends Mary's gift for a particular reason, her act was linked to His burial, and His remark that the poor will always be with them is not a dismissal of the poor. In the Gospels He consistently commands care for them. What is carried forward is the principle that love for Christ may give lavishly, and that giving to Him and giving to the poor are not rivals.

The call to believe in the light while you have it, verses 35 and 36, is addressed to every reader. By contrast the account of hardened hearts is a description of what happened to those who rejected Him, not a verdict on any individual today. No one should read verse 39 as saying a particular person cannot believe.

debates.question: In what sense is the Son of Man glorified through His death?

views.label: The cross is the throne of glory
views.case: John consistently ties glory to the hour of the cross; Jesus is glorified not despite but in His death, where God's love and saving power are most fully revealed, answered by the Father's voice from heaven.

views.label: Glory culminates in resurrection and exaltation
views.case: The lifting up includes exaltation, so the glorification embraces the cross together with the resurrection and ascension that vindicate and enthrone the Son.

debates.bearing: Both belong together in John: the cross itself is the hour of glory, and it flows into the resurrection and exaltation, so that the whole movement of death and rising displays the glory of God.

debates.question: What does it mean that they were unable to believe, per the Isaiah citation?

views.label: Judicial hardening after persistent rejection
views.case: Isaiah 6 describes God confirming in blindness those who have willfully refused the light; their inability follows their sustained refusal, so it is judgment on unbelief, not the cancelling of responsibility.

views.label: The mystery of divine sovereignty and human guilt
views.case: John holds together God's sovereign purpose foretold in Scripture and the real guilt of those who loved human praise more than God's; both are affirmed without being flattened.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage upholds both God's sovereign foreknowledge and the culpability of unbelief, warning readers not to harden themselves against the light while they still have it.

debates.question: Did Mary know she was anointing Jesus for burial?

views.label: She understood what was coming
views.case: Jesus says she has kept the perfume for the day of His burial, and some read that as the insight of one who had listened closely, as she did at His feet in Luke 10:39. The disciples around her missed His talk of death, but she may not have.

views.label: She acted in love, and Jesus gave the act its meaning
views.case: The text does not say Mary spoke of burial, and Mark's account has Jesus say she did what she could, Mark 14:8. On this view her devotion was spontaneous and Jesus interpreted it in light of the cross, which He understood and she did not yet. The disciples remembered the Scripture only after He was glorified, verse 16, and the same may be true of her.

debates.bearing: Either way the lesson is the same. Love that gives itself to Jesus without calculation is more perceptive than it knows, and He uses it for purposes far beyond what the giver sees.

study.originalLanguages:
The crowd's cry 'Hosanna' comes from the Hebrew hoshia na, 'save, we pray,' in Psalm 118:25. It began as a petition and was becoming a shout of praise. John's readers, many of them Greek speakers, would have heard in it both the plea and the promise, and the irony is that the One they hailed is about to answer the plea at the cost of His own life.

The verb hupsoo, 'lift up,' in verse 32 has a double sense that John exploits. It can mean to physically raise and to exalt, and in the Greek Old Testament the Servant of Isaiah 52:13 is the one who will be lifted up and glorified. John then adds in verse 33 that Jesus said this semainon, 'signifying' the kind of death He would die, so that the double meaning is no accident. The verb helkuo, 'draw,' in the same verse also appears in John 6:44, where the Father draws people to the Son, and in John 21:6 of dragging the net full of fish. The cross draws, and what it draws is a catch.

In verse 25 Jesus uses two Greek words for life. The word psyche, the self or soul, is the life one loves and loses. The word zoe, in zoe aionios, eternal life, is the life one keeps. 'Hates' in 'hates his life' is a Semitic way of speaking of a lesser love, as in Luke 14:26, and it does not call for self-loathing. The word apolluei, 'loses,' is the same root as 'perish' in John 3:16.

The kernel of wheat is a kokkos tou sitou, a single grain. Jesus says that if it dies it 'bears much fruit,' using the verb pherei, 'brings,' in the present tense, as a steady fact of the harvest. The word archon in 'prince of this world,' verse 31, means a ruler or leading power, and John uses it again in 14:30 and 16:11. Jesus says he will be cast out, ekblethesetai exo, a word John uses elsewhere for putting someone out of a place, as with the blind man in 9:34 and 35.

Mary's perfume is the object of a verb Jesus chooses carefully. 'She has kept it,' tereo, in verse 7 is the same verb that appears when He says that those who love Him will keep His commandments, John 14:15. The jar was held in reserve for a purpose that was not hers to name. Finally, in verses 39 and 40 John gives Isaiah 6:10 in his own wording. He has Isaiah say that God has 'blinded' and 'hardened,' typhloo and poroo, which differs from the Greek Old Testament and puts the divine action in the foreground.

typology.fulfillment: Messiah and Christ both mean 'Anointed One.' Kings and priests in Israel were anointed with oil on the head, 1 Samuel 16:13, and here the oil is poured on Jesus' feet by a woman who unwittingly prepares Him for burial. The fragrance fills the house, as His death will fill the world with the knowledge of Him. The escalation is that the anointed King is anointed for death, not for a throne, and He reigns by dying. The pattern falls short in this respect: Mary's oil honours the body, while His death accomplishes what no oil could, the forgiveness of sins.

typology.type: The King on a donkey, John 12:14 and 15
typology.fulfillment: Solomon rode David's mule to be crowned, 1 Kings 1:33 to 35, and Zechariah promised a King who is 'righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey,' and who would break the bow of war and proclaim peace to the nations, Zechariah 9:9 and 10. Jesus claims the role on purpose, finding a young donkey and sitting on it. The escalation is that this King's rule extends to the ends of the earth, not by conquest but by the peace His death makes. The type falls short because Solomon's reign ended in division, while this King's reign has no end.

A kernel left alone remains a kernel, but when it falls into the ground and dies it bears much fruit. Jesus applies this first to Himself, and then to His followers in verses 25 and 26. The pattern is that new life comes out of a death that looks like a loss. Paul uses the same picture for resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:36 to 38, and the Greeks' arrival shows the harvest beginning. The picture falls short at one point: a seed's death is natural and automatic, while Jesus' death is a chosen act of love, and the harvest is gathered by His own power.

In the wilderness the bitten Israelites who looked at the bronze snake on a pole lived, Numbers 21:8 and 9, and Jesus has already said the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way, John 3:14 and 15. The correspondence is looking and living. The escalation is that this lifting up is not for one wounded camp but draws everyone, and the cure is not for a snakebite but for sin and death. The type falls short because the bronze serpent was an object that had to be destroyed when it became an idol, 2 Kings 18:4, while the crucified Christ is the one in whom believers live.

study.christ:
The chapter shows Christ as the King who accepts a throne only on His own terms. When the crowd shouts 'Blessed is the King of Israel,' He does not refuse the title, but He chooses a donkey, quietly interpreting kingship in terms of Zechariah's peaceful ruler, and He says at once that His hour means a death. The kingdom comes through the grain of wheat. For John the cross is the coronation.

He is also the Anointed One whose anointing is for the grave. Mary's oil, which Jesus calls preparation for the day of His burial, is a prophecy in action, and John later records that Nicodemus brought a great weight of spices for His body, John 19:38 to 40. Jesus accepts her devotion with a calm that shows He knows where the road leads, and He receives a gift that Judas calls a misuse of money.

He is the Lord of the nations. The Greeks ask to see Him, and He answers by speaking of being lifted up to draw everyone to Himself. Paul says the cross disarmed the powers and put them on public display, Colossians 2:15, and John's 'now the prince of this world will be cast out' announces that victory in advance. The one who is troubled in soul in verse 27 is also the one who rules the outcome.

He is the light. In verses 35 and 36 He urges the crowd to walk while they have the light, and in verse 46 He says, 'I have come into the world as a light, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness.' He is not only a teacher of the light but the light itself, as John 1:4 and 9 and 8:12 say. And in verses 44 and 45 He claims that whoever sees Him sees the One who sent Him, a claim that becomes more explicit in John 14:9.

Isaiah saw His glory, verse 41, which means the Christ of John's Gospel is the Lord of Isaiah 6 who sits on the throne high and exalted. The glory Isaiah saw in the temple is the glory John sees in the cross. This keeps the chapter from becoming sentimental. The man at the dinner table and the King of glory are the same person, and the hour at which He is glorified is the hour He is lifted up.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who speaks from heaven in verse 28, answering the Son's prayer, 'Father, glorify Your name!' with 'I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.' The Father's glory is not an abstraction here. He has already glorified His name in the signs, and He will do so again in the cross and resurrection. John records no voice at Jesus' baptism or on the mount of transfiguration, as the other Gospels do, and this is the only such voice in his Gospel. Jesus says it came for the crowd's sake, verse 30, as a gracious gift of witness for people who would otherwise hear only thunder.

God is shown to be sovereign over unbelief. John does not say that people could not believe because they were not allowed to try. He says they saw many signs and did not believe, verse 37, and then points to Isaiah to show that even this was not outside God's purpose. At the same time many leaders believed but would not confess it, verses 42 and 43, and that is their choice, loving human praise more than the praise of God. The text keeps divine purpose and human responsibility side by side and does not resolve the tension on the reader's behalf.

God is also generous in His judgment. Jesus says He came not to judge but to save the world, verse 47, and that the word He spoke will judge on the last day, verse 48. The standard is not a surprise; it is the word that was spoken in plain hearing. God is the one who sent the Son with a command about what to say and how to say it, verses 49 and 50, and the Son speaks exactly that, so that to hear Him is to hear the Father.

The prince of this world is cast out in this chapter, but not as God's equal. His judgment, verse 31, is promised, and the cross is the instrument. The worship this calls for is quiet confidence. The God who allows the hour to come is the God who plans to glorify His name through it, and who wants His servants to follow where Jesus goes, verse 26, and to receive honour from the Father rather than from people.

crossReferences.note: The prophecy behind the donkey. The King comes humble, brings peace to the nations and breaks the bow of war. John abbreviates the quotation and begins it with 'Do not be afraid,' which echoes Zephaniah 3:16, so that the King's arrival is both a fulfillment and a comfort. The full oracle explains why the nations, represented by the Greeks, appear immediately afterward.

The source of the crowd's cry. The psalm is a procession into the temple of one who comes in the Lord's name, and it was sung at Passover. The people shout it at Jesus without knowing that the stone the builders rejected, Psalm 118:22, is also in the same psalm and describes what is about to happen to Him.

Solomon is set on the king's mule to be anointed and proclaimed. It shows what a king riding a mount meant to Jerusalem's ears: a rightful royal heir, welcomed by a shouting crowd. Jesus' ride repeats the pattern with a deliberate change of mount, from mule to donkey, and a different kind of throne.

Mark's account of the anointing, set in the house of Simon the Leper, has the woman pour the perfume on His head, and Jesus says she has anointed His body in advance of burial and will be remembered wherever the gospel is preached. It confirms that the early church read the act as part of the Passion story.

The earlier promise of the lifting up. As Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes will have eternal life. John 12:32 and 33 repeats the idea and explains it as a death, and the whole Gospel keeps returning to it.

The source of the lifting-up image. Those who looked at the bronze snake on the pole lived. The link lies in the looking: in John, the person who sees the crucified Jesus and believes lives. The older story gives a pattern for how a lifted-up figure can heal those who have been poisoned.

The opening of the Servant song. The Servant is raised, lifted up and highly exalted, and many nations will see what they had not been told. John's lifted up draws on this, and the nations who are startled into silence here are the same nations the Greeks represent in John 12:20.

Isaiah's vision of the Lord on the throne, with the commission to speak to a people who will not turn. John says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory, verse 41, so the glory of the Lord in the temple is the glory of Christ. The hardening of hearts is not a new thing in John's day; it belongs to Isaiah's original calling.

Paul's use of the seed. What is sown does not come to life unless it dies, and God gives it the body He designs. This extends Jesus' own parable in John 12:24 to the believer's resurrection, and shows that the early church heard the grain of wheat as a promise of rising, not only of fruitfulness.

The cross as victory. Having disarmed the powers and authorities, Christ made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross. This is the New Testament commentary on John 12:31, 'the prince of this world will be cast out,' and shows that the lifting up is also a cosmic triumph.

The fulfillment of the Greeks' request. A multitude from every nation, tribe, people and tongue stands before the throne and the Lamb, holding palm branches. The palms that the Jerusalem crowd waved before the cross are in the hands of the harvest in glory.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that has hung over Scripture since Eden: how will the seed of the woman win, and how will the nations be blessed? Abraham was promised that all peoples on earth would be blessed through his offspring, Genesis 12:3. Israel's kings were meant to carry that blessing, and one by one they failed. Zechariah promised a King who would be humble, break the bow of war and speak peace to the nations, and John 12 is where that King finally enters the city.

The arrival of the Greeks is the moment in the story when the nations come asking. What follows is surprising, because He does not receive them but speaks of a grain that must die. The harvest is not gathered by a campaign. It is gathered by a death that makes the seed fruitful. In this way the chapter fills in the mechanism that Isaiah's Servant songs promised without explaining, the Servant who is lifted up and by whom many nations are startled.

The chapter also sets the whole fall into view. The 'prince of this world' is the usurper who gained a hold on creation at the beginning, Genesis 3, and the sentence of judgment on him is announced in verse 31. It is the first note of the sound that will end with Revelation 12:9 to 11, where the accuser is thrown down by the blood of the Lamb. At the other end of the story, the palm branches of Jerusalem reappear in the hands of the countless multitude in Revelation 7:9.

For the reader today, the chapter places us between the shouts and the silence. The crowd that hailed Him on Sunday did not understand what kind of kingdom He was bringing. The kingdom is still being gathered by the seed that fell and died, and the story ends in the new creation where the light is the Lamb and no one walks in darkness, Revelation 21:23.

quiz.q: How does Jesus interpret Mary's anointing of His feet?

options.text: She has kept the perfume in preparation for the day of His burial.
options.note: Verse 7 gives Jesus' own interpretation of her act.

options.text: It was a wasteful act that should have been sold for the poor.
options.note: This was Judas's objection, which sounds charitable but Jesus rejected; the anointing prepared Him for burial.

options.text: It was a beautiful but meaningless gesture.
options.note: Jesus gives it deep meaning, tied to His burial.

options.text: It was an act of costly devotion to Jesus.
options.note: True, but it misses the specific meaning Jesus gives, preparation for His burial.

quiz.q: What does the triumphal entry on a donkey signify?

options.text: Jesus comes as the humble King of Zechariah's prophecy, in peace rather than as a warrior.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 cite Zechariah 9:9, the King on a donkey.

options.text: Jesus was too poor to afford a proper horse.
options.note: The donkey is a deliberate fulfillment of prophecy, not a matter of poverty.

options.text: Jesus rode humbly to show His kingship is not by force.
options.note: There is truth that His reign is not by the sword, but the donkey positively fulfills Zechariah's picture of the coming King.

options.text: Jesus is entering Jerusalem as its King.
options.note: True, but it omits the key note of humility and peace signaled by the donkey.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by the grain of wheat that falls and dies?

options.text: Unless He dies, He remains alone, but through His death He bears the much fruit of many saved.
options.note: Verse 24 pictures His fruitful, saving death.

options.text: That farming requires patience and hard work.
options.note: It is a parable of His death, not agricultural advice.

options.text: That His followers must simply work harder.
options.note: It calls disciples to die to self, verse 25, but its first meaning is Jesus' own death that bears fruit.

options.text: That His death will not be in vain but bear fruit.
options.note: True, but it does not capture that without His death He would remain alone.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say His being lifted up will accomplish?

options.text: He will draw all people to Himself, and the prince of this world will be cast out.
options.note: Verses 31 and 32 describe the cross as cosmic victory and universal drawing.

options.text: He will finally be honored by the religious leaders.
options.note: The lifting up refers to His crucifixion and its saving effect, not the leaders' honor.

options.text: He will ascend to heaven and leave the world behind.
options.note: The lifting up is first the cross; John says it indicates the kind of death He would die.

options.text: He will draw people to Himself through His death.
options.note: True, but it omits the casting out of the prince of this world, the cosmic victory of the cross.

quiz.q: What final appeal does Jesus make as His public ministry closes?

options.text: To believe in the light while they have it, so they may become sons of light.
options.note: Verses 35 and 36 press an urgent call to believe before the darkness comes.

options.text: To wait quietly until the last day for salvation.
options.note: The appeal is urgent and present: believe now, while the light is here.

options.text: To gather more signs before deciding.
options.note: They had already seen many signs; the call is to believe the light now, not seek more proof.

options.text: To walk in the light and not be overtaken by darkness.
options.note: True, but it omits the goal, to become sons of light by believing in the light.

questions: Mary poured out a fortune in love for Jesus while Judas counted the cost. What would extravagant, uncalculating devotion to Christ look like for you?
Jesus embraced His hour rather than praying to be spared it. Where is God calling you to accept a hard path because it is the purpose for which you are there?
A grain of wheat must die to bear fruit. What in your life needs to fall into the ground and die so that God can bring life through you?
Many leaders believed but would not confess Christ because they loved human praise. Whose approval are you most tempted to prize above God's?
Jesus said, believe in the light while you have it. Is there any delay in your response to Him that this urgent call presses you to end today?

translationNotes.note: About a pint of pure nard; the BSB footnote gives a litra, roughly 12 ounces. Worth about three hundred denarii, nearly a year's wages, the perfume was extraordinarily costly.
Hosanna transliterates the Hebrew for Save now, from Psalm 118:25, which became a shout of praise; Blessed is He who comes quotes Psalm 118:26.
See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey quotes Zechariah 9:9, the prophecy of the humble King.
He has blinded their eyes quotes Isaiah 6:10, and verse 38 quotes Isaiah 53:1; John says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory, identifying the Lord of Isaiah 6 with Christ.
